'''Thomas Milton Liggett''' (March 29, 1944 – May 12, 2020) was a mathematician at the [[UCLA|University of California, Los Angeles]]. He worked in [[probability theory]], specializing in [[interacting particle systems]].

==Early life==
Thomas Milton Liggett was born on March 29, 1944, in [[Danville, Kentucky]].<ref name="whoswho">{{Cite book|last1=Vitale|first1=Sarah A.|date=December 1992|title=Who's who in California|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zd0jAQAAIAAJ&q=%22Liggett,+Thomas+Milton%22+AND+%221944%22|isbn=978-1-880142-01-1}}</ref> Liggett moved at the age of two with his missionary parents to Latin America, where he was educated in [[Buenos Aires|Bueno Aires, Argentina]] and [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]]. He graduated from [[Oberlin College]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in 1965, where he was influenced towards [[probability theory|probability]] by Samuel Goldberg (b. 1925), an ex-student of [[William Feller]]. He moved to [[Stanford]], taking classes with [[Kai Lai Chung]], and writing his thesis, ''Weak Convergence of Conditioned Sums of Independent Random Vectors'', in 1969 with advisor [[Samuel Karlin]] on problems associated with the [[Donsker's theorem|invariance principle]]. He graduated with a [[Master of Science]] in 1966 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1969.<ref name="whoswho"/><ref name=TLcv/><ref name="mathgene_m">{{Mathgenealogy|id=36685}}</ref>

==Career==
Liggett joined the faculty at [[UCLA]] in 1969, where he spent his entire career. He became a professor in the mathematics department in 1976, and served as department chair from 1991 to 1994. He retired in 2011, but remained active within the department.<ref name="memoriam">{{Cite web|title=In Memoriam: Thomas M. Liggett|url=https://ww3.math.ucla.edu/in-memoriam-thomas-m-liggett/|website=www.math.ucla.edu|date=2020-05-28|access-date=2021-03-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324041757/https://ww3.math.ucla.edu/in-memoriam-thomas-m-liggett/|archive-date=2022-03-24|url-status=live}}</ref> He was the advisor of [[Norman Matloff]]<ref name="mathgene_m"/> and [[Amber L. Puha]].<ref>{{Mathgenealogy|id=36639}}</ref>

Liggett had contributed to numerous areas of [[probability theory]], including subadditive [[ergodic theory]], [[random graphs]], [[renewal theory]], and was best known for his pioneering work on [[interacting particle systems]], including the [[Contact process (mathematics)|contact process]], the [[voter model]], and the [[exclusion process]].<ref name="google scholar">{{cite web | title = Tom Liggett's publications on Google Scholar | url = https://scholar.google.co.uk/scholar?as_q=&num=10&btnG=Search+Scholar&as_epq=&as_oq=&as_eq=&as_occt=any&as_sauthors=TM+Liggett&as_publication=&as_ylo=&as_yhi=&as_allsubj=some&as_subj=eng&as_subj=phy&hl=en&lr=&safe=off}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Publications of Tom Liggett since 2000 | url=https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tml/post2000pubs.html}}</ref>  His two books in this field have been influential.<ref>{{Cite book | first=T.M. | last=Liggett | title=Interacting Particle Systems | publisher=Springer | year=1985 | isbn=0-387-96069-4 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/interactingparti0000ligg }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book | first=T.M. | last=Liggett | title=Stochastic Interacting Systems: Contact, Voter and Exclusion Processes | publisher=Springer | year = 1999 | isbn=3-540-65995-1}}</ref>

Liggett was the managing editor of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics|Annals of Probability]] from 1985&ndash;1987. He held a [[Sloan Fellowship|Sloan Research Fellowship]] from 1973&ndash;1977, and a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] from 1997&ndash;1998. He was the Wald Memorial Lecturer of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] in 1996, and was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 2008.<ref name=TLcv>{{cite web | title=Tom Liggett's curriculum vitae | url=https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tml/cv.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=UCLA Newsroom, 13 June 2009 | url=http://newsroom.ucla.edu/portal/ucla/three-ucla-professors-receive-49640.aspx}}</ref> He had been elected to the American Academy of Arts & Sciences in 2012,<ref>{{cite web | title=Six UCLA professors elected to American Academy of Arts and Sciences | url=http://newsroom.ucla.edu/portal/ucla/6-ucla-professors-elected-to-american-232149.aspx}}</ref> and in 2012 he also became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-01-27.</ref>

==Personal life==
Liggett married Christina Marie Goodale on August 19, 1972. They had two children, Timothy and Amy.<ref name="whoswho"/> Liggett died on May 12, 2020, in [[Los Angeles]].<ref name="memoriam"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://imstat.org/2020/07/16/obituary-thomas-m-liggett-1944-2020/ |title=Obituary: Thomas M. Liggett 1944–2020 |date=2020-07-16 |last=Durrett |first=Rick |website=imstat.org |access-date=2022-03-24}}</ref>
